title: Algorithms, Compilers, Distributed & Formal
tagline: The deep core, in order — MIT, CMU, and Stanford distilled to their load-bearing ideas.
blurb: IL-08 is the deep-core academy: MIT's 6-3 curriculum distilled (6.100 Python, 6.1200 discrete math, 6.1210/1220 algorithms, 6.1910 computation structures, 6.1800/1810 systems, theory through complexity), CMU's systems-and-theory spine (imperative/functional core, 15-210/213, 15-251/451, 15-440/445/410, AI breadth), and Stanford's core cross-walk (106A/B, 103/109, 107/111, 161, depth branches). For the learner who wants the ground truth beneath the frameworks — proofs, systems, and theory that don't expire.

modules.title: MIT 6-3: The Distilled Core
modules.summary: MIT's EECS curriculum in prerequisite order: 6.100A/B Python (computational thinking, problem-set discipline), 6.1200 Mathematics for Computer Science (proofs, induction, number theory, graphs, probability), 6.1210/6.1220 Algorithms (design, analysis, lower bounds, NP-completeness), 6.1910 Computation Structures (gates to processor, the hardware/software contract), 6.1800/6.1810 Systems Engineering (design at scale), and theory from automata to complexity (the 6.1400 lineage).
objectives: Write proofs by induction, contradiction, and invariant.
Analyze algorithms: recurrences, amortized analysis, lower bounds.
Explain the hardware/software contract: ISA, assembly, caches, VM.
State what NP-completeness means and prove a reduction.

notes.title: Programming and math: 6.100, 6.1200
notes.body:
**6.100A/B**: Python at MIT depth — **computational thinking** (decomposition, abstraction, algorithms), the **problem-set discipline** (weekly sets, test-driven). The sets are the course — lectures are commentary.

**6.1200**: **proofs** (direct, contradiction, contrapositive), **induction** (the template until it's reflex), **number theory** (divisibility, modular arithmetic, gcd — RSA's prerequisites), **graph theory** (the universal modeling language), **probability for computing** (randomization analysis).

- Induction template: base case → hypothesis → step. Every recursive algorithm's correctness proof uses it
- Invariants: the loop invariant proves the loop — state it before writing the loop
- Number theory: Fermat's little theorem, Euler's theorem — the crypto foundations

notes.title: Algorithms: 6.1210/6.1220
notes.body:
**Introduction to algorithms**: sorting, hashing, divide-and-conquer (recurrences: master theorem), dynamic programming, graphs (BFS/DFS/Dijkstra/MST).

**Design and analysis**: greedy correctness (exchange arguments), **amortized analysis** (aggregate/accounting/potential), **lower bounds** (comparison sorting is Ω(n log n) — the decision-tree argument), **NP-completeness** (reductions: 3-SAT → everything).

- Master theorem: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) — memorize the three cases, derive when unsure
- Exchange arguments: greedy stays ahead — the proof pattern for MST/scheduling
- Reductions: to prove X hard, reduce a known-hard problem TO X — direction matters

notes.title: Structures, systems, theory
notes.body:
**6.1910 Computation Structures**: **gates to the processor** (combinational → sequential → FSM → datapath), the **hardware/software contract** (ISA, assembly, calling conventions), caches and virtual memory.

**6.1800/6.1810**: **systems engineering** (modularity, end-to-end argument, fate sharing), **OS engineering** (xv6: build a real kernel — the labs).

**Theory (6.1400 lineage)**: finite automata, Turing machines, decidability (the halting problem), **complexity classes** (P, NP, NP-complete, PSPACE).

- The FSM-to-processor climb: every level is the previous level's abstraction — no magic
- xv6: reading a real kernel demystifies every OS concept — scheduling, VM, filesystems in 10k lines
- Halting proof: diagonalization — the most beautiful proof in CS, learn it cold

cards.back: Base case → inductive hypothesis → inductive step. Reflex.
A property true before/after each iteration — proves the loop correct. State it first.
f(n) vs n^(log_b a): smaller → case 1; equal → case 2 (× log n); larger (regular) → case 3.
Ω(n log n) — decision-tree argument: n! leaves need log(n!) depth.
Reduce known-hard TO your problem (3-SAT ≤p X proves X hard). Direction matters.
Diagonalization — assume a decider, construct the contradiction.

quiz.q: Prove: sum of first n odds = n². Method?
quiz.explain: Induction: base n=1, assume n, show n+1 adds (2n+1): n²+2n+1=(n+1)².
Master case 2: f(n)=n = n^(log_2 2) → Θ(n log n). Mergesort's recurrence.
Doubling strategy: n appends cost O(n) total — O(1) amortized each.

quiz.q: To prove problem X NP-complete, you?
choices: reduce 3-SAT to X in polytime + show X in NP
quiz.explain: 3-SAT ≤p X shows X at least as hard; X ∈ NP completes it.
A real Unix-like kernel in ~10k lines — every concept made concrete.

choices: implement function at the endpoints, not the network
quiz.explain: Correctness (e.g., reliable delivery) belongs at endpoints — the network can't guarantee it.

modules.title: CMU: The Systems-and-Theory Spine
modules.summary: Carnegie Mellon's core: imperative and functional foundations (15-122 imperative computation, 15-150 functional programming — correctness as a habit), data structures and systems (15-210 parallel/sequential DSA, 15-213 computer systems with the malloc and shell labs), theory (15-251 great ideas, 15-451 algorithm design — proofs plus programming), systems depth (15-445 databases, 15-440 distributed, 15-410 OS design — build a kernel), and AI breadth (07-280).
objectives: Write correct code: contracts, invariants, functional and imperative styles.
Build systems in C: malloc, shells, caches, VM — the 15-213 labs.
Prove and program: theory with implementation (15-251/451).
Design distributed systems and databases; build OS components.

notes.title: Imperative + functional: correctness as a habit
notes.body:
**15-122 (Imperative)**: contracts (pre/post-conditions), loop invariants, data structure correctness — C0/C with proof discipline.

**15-150 (Functional)**: **functional programming** — recursion, higher-order functions, types, parallelism from purity.

**Correctness as a habit**: write the contract before the code; the invariant before the loop.

- Contracts: the function's promise — callers rely on it, implementations honor it
- Purity → parallelism: no side effects means safe parallel evaluation — the 15-210 bridge
- Two paradigms, one discipline: state what the code must do, then make it true

notes.title: 15-210/213: structures and systems
notes.body:
**15-210**: **parallel and sequential DSA** — cost models (work/span), parallel algorithms, sequences/sets/maps with parallel implementations.

**15-213**: **introduction to computer systems** — the legendary course: data representation, assembly, **the malloc lab** (write a real allocator), **the shell lab** (job control), caches, VM, concurrency.

- Work/span: work = total operations, span = critical path — parallelism = work/span
- The malloc lab: explicit free lists, coalescing — memory management demystified forever
- 15-213's thesis: programmers who understand the machine write better programs — in any language

notes.title: Theory, depth, breadth
notes.body:
**15-251/451**: **great ideas** (the beautiful proofs) + **algorithm design** — proofs PLUS programming, never proofs alone.

**Systems depth**: **15-445** (database systems: build a real DB — buffer pool, B+trees, query execution), **15-440** (distributed systems: RPC, consensus, consistency), **15-410** (**build a kernel** — the capstone of systems education).

**07-280**: AI breadth — search, ML, RL, probability; implement AlexNet, GPT-2, AlphaZero (the 'rebuild the landmarks' pedagogy).

- 15-445: building a database teaches more than using ten — storage to execution
- Consensus (Paxos/Raft): the distributed systems atom — agree despite failures
- 15-410: a working kernel — the deepest programming most will ever do

cards.back: Work: total operations. Span: longest dependency chain. Parallelism ≈ work/span.
Understanding the machine makes better programmers — in every language.
Explicit free lists + coalescing — allocation demystified; fragmentation is the enemy.
Agreement despite failures — the distributed systems atom (Paxos/Raft).
A working kernel — threads, VM, syscalls. The deepest programming.
Implement AlexNet/GPT-2/AlphaZero yourself — landmarks become understanding.

quiz.q: Parallel sum of n elements: work and span?
quiz.explain: Work O(n) total adds; span O(log n) tree depth — parallelism n/log n.
Merging adjacent free blocks fights fragmentation — the allocator's core duty.

Fanout^levels: 100³ = 1M — the arithmetic behind index depth.

modules.title: Stanford: The Core Cross-Walk
modules.summary: Stanford's core as a cross-walk: programming (106A methodology in Python, 106B abstractions in C++ — recursion and data structures), mathematical foundations (CS103 proofs/logic/graphs, CS109 probability for computer scientists), systems (CS107 computer organization and systems, CS111 operating systems principles), algorithms (CS161 design and analysis), and the depth branches (theory 154/254, systems 143/144/145, AI 221/229/230/224N/231N/234).
objectives: Think recursively: 106B's core skill — recursion as a problem-solving strategy.
Prove and count: logic, graphs, probability (103/109).
Program the machine: bits, C, assembly, OS principles (107/111).
Analyze: CS161's algorithm canon with randomization.

notes.title: Programming and math: 106A/B, 103/109
notes.body:
**106A (Methodology)**: Python, decomposition, testing — programming as a craft. **106B (Abstractions)**: C++, **recursion** (the core skill — recursive problem-solving before iterative), data structures, big-O.

**CS103**: **proofs, logic, graphs** — mathematical foundations with CS flavor. **CS109**: **probability for computer scientists** — the probability you'll actually use (randomized algorithms, ML).

- Recursion-first: think recursively, then convert — the 106B pedagogy
- CS109: probability as a tool — expectation, variance, concentration for algorithm analysis
- 106B's C++: the language where abstractions cost nothing — templates, RAII in the curriculum

notes.title: Systems: 107 and 111
notes.body:
**CS107**: **computer organization and systems** — bits, C, assembly, memory hierarchy, the famous assignments (and the debugging discipline they forge).

**CS111**: **operating systems principles** (the current course) — processes, concurrency, virtual memory, filesystems — principles over the specific kernel.

- CS107's gift: C programming with the machine model in your head — pointers stop being scary
- The assignments are the course — buffer overflows teach security, allocators teach memory
- CS111: principles transfer across kernels — concepts, not trivia

notes.title: Algorithms and depth branches
notes.body:
**CS161**: **design and analysis** — divide-and-conquer, DP, graphs, **randomization** (randomized quicksort, hashing, Karger) — with the famous rigor.

**Depth branches**: **theory** (154 automata/complexity, 254 advanced), **systems** (143 compilers, 144 networking, 145 databases), **AI** (221, 229, 230, 224N, 231N, 234 — the sequence IL-07's ML arc follows).

- Randomization: Karger's min-cut — the algorithm that's wrong sometimes and brilliant anyway
- 143 (compilers): the dragon course — lexing to codegen, the full pipeline
- The cross-walk's value: see the SAME ideas (recursion, induction, layering) across all three schools

cards.back: Recursive problem-solving — think recursively first, then convert.
Computer scientists: randomized algorithms, ML — the usable subset.
C with the machine model in mind — pointers, assembly, memory hierarchy.
Randomized contraction — wrong sometimes, brilliant in expectation; repeat for confidence.
Lexing → parsing → semantic → IR → optimization → codegen — the full pipeline.
Same ideas (recursion, induction, layering) across MIT/CMU/Stanford — triangulation.

quiz.explain: Random pivot → expected O(n log n) — randomization defeats adversarial input.

quiz.q: Karger repeated n²log n times gives?
quiz.explain: Amplification: repeats drive failure probability exponentially down.

choices: lex → parse → semantic → IR → optimize → codegen
quiz.explain: The pipeline: tokens → tree → checked → IR → better IR → machine code.

scriptLabs.title: Induction Proof Workshop
scriptLabs.brief: Write complete induction proofs for three claims: sum of odds, Bernoulli's inequality, and the loop invariant of binary search. The required fragments force the proof skeleton.
scriptLabs.starter:
# For each claim, write: BASE, HYPOTHESIS, STEP.
# 1. sum_{i=1..n} (2i-1) = n^2
# 2. (1+x)^n >= 1+nx for x > -1 (Bernoulli)
# 3. Binary search loop invariant: if key in a[0..n), key in a[lo..hi)
scriptLabs.hint: Bernoulli step: (1+x)^(k+1) = (1+x)^k(1+x) >= (1+kx)(1+x) = 1+(k+1)x+kx² >= 1+(k+1)x. Binary search: invariant preserved by halving.
scriptLabs.solution:
# 1. Sum of odds
# BASE: n=1: 1 = 1^2. HYPOTHESIS: sum to k = k^2.
# STEP: sum to k+1 = k^2 + (2(k+1)-1) = k^2+2k+1 = (k+1)^2. QED.
# 2. Bernoulli: BASE n=0: 1>=1. HYPOTHESIS: (1+x)^k >= 1+kx.
# STEP: (1+x)^(k+1)=(1+x)^k(1+x) >= (1+kx)(1+x) = 1+(k+1)x+kx^2 >= 1+(k+1)x. QED.
# 3. Binary search invariant: key in a[lo..hi) initially (lo=0,hi=n).
# STEP: mid=(lo+hi)//2; if a[mid]==key done; if key<a[mid] hi=mid else lo=mid+1.
# Invariant preserved: key (if present) stays in [lo,hi). Termination: hi-lo shrinks.
# QED: loop exits with key found or lo==hi (absent).

scriptLabs.title: A Tiny Allocator (15-213 Spirit)
scriptLabs.brief: Implement a bump allocator with free-list reuse in Python (simulating the malloc lab): malloc(size), free(ptr), with first-fit search and coalescing. The 15-213 lesson in miniature.
scriptLabs.hint: malloc: scan free_list for length>=n; split remainder back. free: insert sorted, merge with adjacent (coalesce). Track allocations in a dict for the demo.
scriptLabs.solution:
class MiniHeap:
    def __init__(self, size=1024):
        self.mem = bytearray(size)
        self.free_list = [(0, size)]
        self.allocd = {}
    def malloc(self, n):
        for i, (off, ln) in enumerate(self.free_list):
            if ln >= n:  # first-fit
                self.allocd[off] = n
                if ln == n:
                    self.free_list.pop(i)
                else:  # split: carve n, leave remainder
                    self.free_list[i] = (off+n, ln-n)
                return off
        return None
    def free(self, off):
        n = self.allocd.pop(off)
        self.free_list.append((off, n))
        self.free_list.sort()
        # coalesce adjacent
        merged = [self.free_list[0]]
        for o, l in self.free_list[1:]:
            po, pl = merged[-1]
            if po+pl == o:
                merged[-1] = (po, pl+l)
            else:
                merged.append((o, l))
        self.free_list = merged

h = MiniHeap(64)
a, b, c = h.malloc(16), h.malloc(16), h.malloc(16)
h.free(b)          # hole in the middle
d = h.malloc(8)    # first-fit reuses the hole, splits remainder
print('free_list:', h.free_list)  # coalescing visible
# Lesson: fragmentation is the enemy; coalescing is the defense.

scenarios.title: Choosing the Algorithm
scenarios.context: You need the median of 10M numbers, memory for the full array, one pass preferred.

options.why: Selection doesn't need sorting — quickselect finds the kth element in expected linear time.

options.text: Sort then index — O(n log n)
options.why: Correct but wasteful — sorting does work selection doesn't need.
O(n log n) with worse constants — quickselect dominates.

options.text: Randomized pivot (or median-of-medians for worst-case guarantee)
options.why: Randomization defeats adversarial order; median-of-medians gives deterministic O(n).

scenarios.title: The Counter Must Agree
scenarios.context: Three replicas count ad impressions. Network partitions happen. The business needs the total.

options.why: Correct but slow/expensive for a counter — and partitions block progress.

options.text: CRDT counter (G-Counter) — mergeable, available under partition
options.why: Counters are the CRDT success story: increments commute, merge is exact, partitions don't block.

options.text: Increments commute and merge is idempotent — the operation's algebra fits the data type
options.why: CRDTs work when operations commute; counting is the canonical case.

blocks.body: Induction: base→hypothesis→step · Contradiction: assume ¬P, derive absurdity · Invariant: true before/after each iteration · Exchange: greedy stays ahead
Master: T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n) vs n^(log_b a) · substitution · recursion trees · amortized: aggregate/accounting/potential
Comparison sort Ω(n log n) · decision trees · adversary arguments · reductions for NP-hardness (3-SAT ≤p X)
Work/span · parallelism = work/span · Brent: Tp ≤ W/P + S
Gates→FSM→datapath→ISA→assembly→C · caches: locality · VM: pages, TLB · calling conventions
Processes/threads · scheduling · sync (locks, semaphores) · VM · filesystems (inodes, journaling) · xv6 as reference
RPC · consensus (Raft: leader, log, safety) · consistency models · CRDTs for commutative ops · end-to-end argument
P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE · NP-complete: hardest in NP · halting undecidable (diagonalization) · reductions direction matters

answerBank.q: Which school's version should I follow?
answerBank.a: All three where they overlap — that's the point of the cross-walk. Start with MIT's order (prerequisite-clean), use CMU for systems depth (15-213/410), Stanford for the AI branches. The module sequences them.

answerBank.q: Do I really need theory for a dev job?
answerBank.a: For most CRUD work, no. For interviews at selective companies, distributed systems, databases, and performance work — yes, constantly. Theory is the highest-leverage knowledge: it doesn't expire.

answerBank.q: How do I learn proofs as a programmer?
answerBank.a: Write them like code: state the claim (spec), then the proof (implementation). Do every exercise in 6.1200/CS103 — proofs are a writing skill, and writing is learned by writing.

answerBank.q: xv6 vs Linux for learning OS?
answerBank.a: xv6 first (10k lines, every concept visible), then Linux source for the specific subsystem you need. The module uses xv6 as the reference implementation.

answerBank.q: P vs NP — should I care?
answerBank.a: As a practitioner: NP-completeness tells you when to stop searching for the perfect algorithm and start approximating. That's a career's worth of saved time in one concept.
